section: Standard Error of averaged player estimates
text:
Standard Error of averaged player estimates
This is essentially says how much does a players’ performance vary, how consistent of a performer are they? This interpretation is sensible for players with more than 5 games played and tells you who the steady performers are, we can see a strong correlation between the number of games played and the standard error of the a players’ ability/strength score. However, for players with stronger shrinkage there is a caveat. Their ability/strength scores will vary less because of how the model is designed with a harsher shrinkage parameter

title: Under Maintenance…
text:
Network
Why is this network graph of interest? The comparison graph with players as nodes and a directed edge from each match winner to the loser helps determine whether maximum likelihood estimation is even well-defined. If the comparison graph is not strongly connected, meaning every player is linked to every other by a directed path of wins, we risk our estimates diverging when performing MLE. Our graph does not satisfy this condition, so some ability estimates would diverge under pure MLE. This motivated our use of Maximum A Posteriori estimation, whose prior acts as a regulariser and guarantees finite, unique estimates regardless of the graph’s connectivity.

section: Optimisation Curve Illustrating flatness around minimum
text:
Optimisation Curve Illustrating flatness around minimum
The reason for not choosing the absolute minimum but taking a point nearby is explained in more depth in section 3.3 of the full report. The plot here shows that the curve is flat around the minimum which means if we change our choice of hyperparameters the log loss we are trying to minimise does not change in a significant way.
